15700: Taffeta is a type of fabric — a woven cloth used to make clothing and home furnishings. What makes it stand out from most other fabrics is its combination of three qualities happening all at once: it is crisp, smooth, and shiny. Most fabrics are either soft and drapey (like satin or silk charmeuse) or stiff and matte (like canvas). Taffeta sits in its own category — it has body and structure, meaning it holds its shape rather than hanging limply, and yet it also has a lustrous, almost glass-like sheen on its surface.

Taffeta has a smooth, polished surface that reflects light clearly, giving it a bright, elegant shine. It is not flashy or mirror-like; it's more like the quiet glow of a pearl. The fabric often looks opulent and rich, which is why it is associated with formal and special-occasion wear.

One of the most recognisable visual features of taffeta is something called shot taffeta (also called changeable taffeta or iridescent taffeta). This happens when the threads running in one direction are a different colour from the threads running in the other direction. When light hits such a fabric from different angles, it appears to shift and change colour — a blue-and-green taffeta might look blue from one side of the room and green from another. This colour-shifting quality is considered beautiful and is a hallmark of high-quality taffeta.

Run your hand over taffeta and you'll notice it feels smooth, cool, and slightly stiff — almost like a very fine, flexible paper. This stiffness is not roughness; it doesn't scratch you. Rather, the fabric has resistance — it pushes back a little instead of collapsing like a soft cloth. This quality is called crispness in fabric terminology, and taffeta is one of the crispest fabrics in common use.

Because of this crispness, taffeta holds its shape very well. If you scrunch it in your hand, it will likely crease (taffeta creases and wrinkles fairly easily, which is a known drawback), but when laid flat or worn, it maintains structure on its own. A skirt made of taffeta will puff outward rather than draping close to the body. This body-giving quality is prized in formal dressmaking.

This is one of the most charming and recognisable things about taffeta: it rustles. When someone wearing a taffeta garment walks or moves, the fabric makes a soft, whispering, swishing sound — a subtle "swish-swish." This sound is so associated with taffeta (and silk taffeta especially) that it even has its own technical name: scroop. In literature and in real life, the rustling of a taffeta gown often signals elegance, ceremony, or luxury. No other common fabric produces quite this sound as reliably.

Taffeta was historically made from pure silk — the natural fibre produced by silkworms. Silk taffeta is considered the finest and most prestigious form of the fabric. It is lighter, softer to the touch, and has a more subtle, natural sheen than its synthetic cousins.

Today, most taffeta sold and used in clothing is made from synthetic fibres, primarily polyester or nylon. Synthetic taffeta is more affordable, easier to care for, and widely available. It tends to be slightly stiffer and more plastic-feeling than silk taffeta, and its sheen can appear brighter or more artificial. When people refer to taffeta in everyday conversation — say, in describing a prom dress or a bridesmaid's gown — they are almost always referring to synthetic (usually polyester) taffeta.

Some taffeta is blended — made from a mix of silk and synthetic fibres — to balance cost with quality.

Beyond the basic form, there are a few well-known varieties:

Shot taffeta (changeable taffeta): As described above, it uses two different colours of thread, creating an iridescent, colour-shifting effect.

Moiré taffeta: This variety has a distinctive pattern pressed into it that resembles the rippling, watermark-like patterns you sometimes see on water or the inside of a shell. The pattern is created by running the fabric through rollers that apply pressure in a wave-like design. Moiré taffeta has a subtle, almost hypnotic visual texture.

Paper taffeta: An especially thin, lightweight version of taffeta that feels almost like stiff tissue paper. It is very delicate and used primarily for special decorative purposes or very fine couture garments.

Yarn-dyed taffeta: The threads are dyed before weaving, which creates deeper, more consistent colour and often results in slightly richer-looking fabric.

Taffeta is primarily associated with formal and special-occasion clothing. The most common places you'll see it:

  • Ball gowns and evening gowns: The fabric's stiffness creates the full, dramatic skirts associated with formal dresses. It doesn't need multiple layers of petticoats to hold its shape.
  • Wedding dresses: Both for the gown itself and for bridesmaid dresses. The structured look and sheen photograph beautifully.
  • Prom dresses: Probably the most common context in which young people encounter taffeta today.
  • Linings: Taffeta is frequently used as the lining inside jackets, coats, and suits. Here, the smooth, slippery surface makes it easy to slide the garment on and off over other clothes. You may have felt taffeta without realising it — if you've ever put on a formal blazer and felt a cool, smooth, slightly slippery inner surface, that was likely taffeta.
  • Ribbons and accessories: Taffeta ribbons are common in gift-wrapping, hair accessories, and decorative bows because the fabric holds its shape well when tied.
  • Home décor: Curtains, decorative cushion covers, and table runners sometimes use taffeta for its elegant appearance.
How it differs from similar fabrics

To sharpen your understanding, here is how taffeta compares to a few fabrics it is sometimes confused with:

Satin is also shiny and smooth, but satin is soft and drapey — it falls and flows against the body. Taffeta is stiffer and more structured. If satin is like water, taffeta is like a thin sheet of polished cardboard.

Organza is another crisp, sheer fabric used in formal wear, but organza is transparent (you can see through it), whereas taffeta is fully opaque.

Silk charmeuse is a lightweight silk with a beautiful drape and sheen, but again, it falls softly — no crispness or rustling.

The defining combination that makes taffeta taffeta and nothing else is: crisp + smooth + shiny + rustling. If a fabric has all four, it is taffeta.

Taffeta is a crisp, smooth, lustrous fabric with a characteristic rustle when worn. Originally made from silk, it is now commonly made from polyester. It holds its shape rather than draping softly, making it ideal for structured formal garments like ball gowns, wedding dresses, and prom dresses. It is also used as a lining fabric and in decorative applications. Its defining qualities — the sheen, the stiffness, and that distinctive swishing sound — make it one of the most recognisable fabrics in the world of clothing and fashion.
15701: The word tailgate has two main meanings as a verb, used in very different situations. Understanding both will give you a complete picture of the word.
Meaning 1: Driving dangerously close to the car in front of you

This is by far the most common use of tailgate as a verb.

When you are driving, there should always be a safe gap between your car and the car ahead of you — enough space to brake safely if the front car suddenly stops. When a driver tailgates, they ignore this gap and drive so close behind the vehicle in front that there is barely any space between the two cars.

Think of it this way: imagine you are walking behind someone, and you are so close that your feet almost step on their heels with every step. That is essentially what tailgating is — but with cars.

Examples:

  • "The truck behind me kept tailgating me on the highway, even though I was already going at the speed limit."
  • "Stop tailgating! If I hit the brakes suddenly, you'll crash right into me."
  • "He was tailgating me so aggressively that I had to pull over and let him pass."

Why is this dangerous?

When a driver tailgates, they give themselves almost no reaction time. If the car ahead brakes suddenly — say, because an animal runs across the road or traffic suddenly slows — the tailgating driver will not have enough distance to stop in time, causing a rear-end collision. This is why tailgating is considered both reckless and aggressive driving. In many countries, it is also illegal and can result in a fine.

Tailgating is also often used as a form of intimidation on the road. If a driver wants the person in front to go faster or move out of the lane, they might tailgate as a way of pressuring them. This is a recognized form of road aggression.

Related expressions you might hear:

  • "riding someone's bumper" — same idea; a bumper is the part at the front/back of a car
  • "on my tail" — if someone is "on your tail," they are tailgating you
Meaning 2: To have an outdoor social gathering before a sporting event

In American English, tailgate also works as a verb meaning to have an informal, festive gathering in a parking lot — usually right before a big sporting event like an American football or baseball game.

This tradition comes from the culture of opening the tailgate (the hinged panel at the back of a pickup truck), setting up food and drinks on it, and socializing with fellow fans before the game begins. Over time, the noun became a verb.

Examples:

  • "We got to the stadium two hours early to tailgate with our friends before the game."
  • "They tailgated every Sunday during football season."
  • "The whole parking lot was full of people tailgating — grilling burgers, playing music, and wearing their team's jerseys."

A tailgate gathering typically involves grilling food (burgers, hot dogs, etc.), drinking, playing music, and enjoying the excitement of an upcoming event together. It is as much a social ritual as it is about the game itself. While the tradition started with pickup trucks, today people tailgate with any kind of vehicle — SUVs, minivans, even tents set up in parking lots.

This verb is mostly used in American contexts. If you are reading about American sports culture and see phrases like "tailgating before the Super Bowl" or "we tailgated all afternoon," this is what it means.
Meaning 3: Sneaking into a secure area by closely following someone (less common, but important)

There is a third, more specialized use of tailgate that you are likely to encounter in the context of workplace security, cybersecurity awareness, or access control.

When entry to a building or restricted area requires a keycard, PIN, or badge, an unauthorized person might wait for a legitimate employee to open the door and then quickly slip in behind them before the door closes. This act is called tailgating — just as in the driving meaning, the idea is of following too closely, except here the consequence is unauthorized entry rather than a road accident.

Examples:

  • "A stranger tailgated into the office building by walking closely behind an employee who had just scanned their badge."
  • "The security training warned employees not to let anyone tailgate through restricted doors, even if the person looks familiar."
  • "The breach happened because someone tailgated into the server room."

This form of tailgating is a known security threat, and organizations specifically train employees to watch out for it. The polite but correct thing to do is to ask the person behind you to use their own credentials rather than letting them in.

SituationWhat "tailgate" means
On the roadDrive dangerously close behind another vehicle
Before a sports eventHave a festive outdoor party in a parking lot
At a secure buildingSneak in through a controlled door by closely following an authorized person
One final note on tone and register

Tailgating (the driving behaviour) carries a strongly negative tone. If someone says "that driver was tailgating me," they are almost certainly frustrated or alarmed. It is never seen as acceptable or skillful driving — it is always reckless.

Tailgating (the social gathering) carries a positive, festive tone. It is something people look forward to and talk about with enthusiasm.

Tailgating (the security breach) is neutral to negative — it describes an act that is considered a vulnerability or a violation of security rules.

Knowing the context will always make the correct meaning obvious.
15702:
A tailspin is what happens when a plane loses control and starts falling from the sky — not in a straight line, but in a tight, rapid, spinning spiral. The nose of the plane points downward, and the tail swings around and around as the whole aircraft corkscrews toward the ground. The pilot is not in control. The plane is not simply dropping — it is spinning and falling at the same time, and every second that passes makes it harder to recover.

That image — something spinning rapidly out of control, falling fast, getting worse by the moment — is the heart of this word.
What It Means in Everyday Life

In everyday use, a tailspin means a situation of sudden, rapid, and uncontrolled decline — one that is very difficult to stop or reverse.

The key ideas packed into this word are:

  1. Speed — things go wrong fast.
  2. Loss of control — nobody is steering anymore; the situation has taken over.
  3. A spiral effect — each bad thing makes the next bad thing worse. The problems feed on each other, the way a spinning plane spins faster as it falls.
  4. Difficulty of recovery — just like a pilot struggling to pull out of a tailspin, whatever is in a tailspin is hard to bring back to stability.

This word is used for a wide range of situations — emotional, financial, personal, organizational, and more.

Here are examples that show how the word feels and functions:

  • Emotional / personal:

"After losing his job, he went into a tailspin — he stopped sleeping, stopped eating, and withdrew from everyone."
(One bad thing — losing the job — triggered a rapid, uncontrolled spiral of worsening emotional states.)

  • Financial / business:

"The company entered a tailspin after the scandal broke. Investors pulled out, employees started leaving, and sales collapsed within weeks."
(Notice the chain reaction — one event caused another, which caused another. That spiral is exactly what 'tailspin' captures.)

  • National / large-scale:

"The economy went into a tailspin during the crisis, with unemployment and inflation rising simultaneously."

  • Relationship:

"Their marriage entered a tailspin after the argument — small misunderstandings grew into major fights every single day."

You almost never see "tailspin" standing alone. It almost always appears with specific verbs and prepositions. Here are the most natural, commonly used combinations:

PhraseMeaning
go into a tailspinto begin an uncontrolled downward spiral
send (something/someone) into a tailspinto cause something to suddenly start spiraling out of control
enter a tailspina slightly more formal version of "go into a tailspin"
be in a tailspinto currently be in that uncontrolled, declining state
pull out of a tailspinto successfully recover and regain control after a period of rapid decline

Examples:

  • "The bad news sent the stock market into a tailspin."
  • "It took her two years to pull out of the tailspin she fell into after her divorce."
  • "The team has been in a tailspin since they lost three games in a row."
What Makes a "Tailspin" Different from a Simple "Decline"

This is an important distinction.

If you say "the company's profits declined," that's neutral. It could mean profits dropped a little, slowly, or steadily.

But if you say "the company went into a tailspin," you are saying something much more dramatic:

  • The decline was fast
  • It was out of control
  • It likely snowballed — one problem made other problems appear
  • Recovery is not obvious or easy

Similarly, "downfall" describes an end result. "Tailspin" describes the process — the chaotic, spinning, worsening journey toward that end result.

"Tailspin" is a vivid, somewhat dramatic word. Because it comes from an image of a crashing airplane, it carries a sense of urgency and alarm.

  • It is used in both formal writing (news articles, business reports) and everyday conversation.
  • It is always negative — you will never hear "going into a tailspin" used to describe something good.
  • It signals that the speaker views the situation as serious, fast-moving, and potentially catastrophic.

A tailspin is a rapid, uncontrolled, and self-worsening downward spiral — in a person's emotions, a company's fortunes, a relationship, or any situation — where things are deteriorating fast, control has been lost, and recovery requires real effort.

That's the full picture of "tailspin" — from airplane to everyday life, with all the texture and nuance of how the word actually lives and breathes in the English language.
15703:
A taint is a small but damaging trace of something bad — such as corruption, wrongdoing, disease, or moral pollution — that sticks to a person, thing, or reputation and spoils it, even if just slightly.

Think of it like a drop of ink in a glass of clean water. The ink is tiny, but it changes the water. You can no longer call it purely clean. That is exactly what a taint does — it doesn't have to be a massive, overwhelming stain. It just needs to be there, and its presence is enough to corrupt, mark, or spoil.

A few things make this word unique and precise:

It suggests something that lingers. A taint isn't a one-time offense that disappears. It clings. It follows a person or thing around and is difficult to shake off, even long after the original bad event.

It implies contamination. Like a physical contamination (a spoiled ingredient in food), a taint suggests that something which was once clean, honest, or good has now been infected by something negative.

It can be very small, but still destructive. The word specifically captures that in-between state — not completely ruined, but no longer fully clean either. A hint of badness that compromises the whole.

It carries a heavy moral weight. Even when the taint is small, it is taken seriously because it calls into question the purity, honesty, or integrity of whatever it is attached to.
The Different Contexts Where It Appears

1. Reputation and character
This is the most common use. A person's reputation can carry a taint if they were ever connected to something shameful, even if they weren't fully responsible.

"Even after he was cleared, there was still a taint of suspicion around his name."

Here, the suspicion is not proven, but it exists as a trace — a shadow — and that's enough to damage how people see him.

2. Corruption and institutions
Organizations, governments, or systems can be described as having a taint when there is evidence of wrongdoing that poisons the whole structure.

"The taint of corruption had spread through the entire department."

3. Food, biology, and disease (literal use)
In a more physical sense, taint refers to contamination — like when food is slightly spoiled or a disease has entered a population.

"The taint in the meat made it unsafe to eat."

This usage is a bit older and more formal, but it is still encountered in writing.

4. Legal contexts
In law, a taint refers to the contaminating effect of illegal or improper actions on otherwise valid evidence or proceedings.

"The taint from the illegal search affected the entire case."

In law, this is quite serious — a taint can make whole batches of evidence inadmissible because the original wrongdoing has "infected" everything connected to it.

• A taint is almost always undesirable and negative. You will never hear someone say "a taint of kindness" or "a taint of happiness." It is always associated with something bad.
  • The word implies that the damage is hard or impossible to undo. Once there is a taint, the original clean state is gone.
  • A taint doesn't need to be proven or visible to exist. Even a suspicion of wrongdoing can be described as a taint.
  • It is often used to describe something that was previously respected or clean and has now been compromised. The word always implies there was a "before" state that was better.

In casual, informal (and somewhat crude) usage, "taint" is also a slang term for the perineum — the area of the body between the genitals and the anus. This meaning is widely known in informal English, especially in American usage. It is considered vulgar or rude in formal settings, so you would only encounter it in casual conversation or comedy — not in newspapers, academic writing, or professional contexts.

In short, as a noun, taint means a trace or mark of something bad — corruption, wrongdoing, disease, or disgrace — that contaminates or spoils a person, place, institution, or thing. It suggests something subtle but persistent, something that sticks around and is hard to clean away, and it always implies that what was once clean or good has been compromised. Its additional informal meaning refers to a specific part of the human anatomy, used only in casual or crude speech.
15704:
To taint something means to introduce something bad into something that was clean, pure, or good — corrupting it, spoiling it, or making it untrustworthy as a result.

Think of it like a single drop of ink falling into a glass of clear water. The ink doesn't need to fill the whole glass to ruin it. Just one drop spreads through everything and makes the whole glass something you no longer want to drink. That is the essence of taint. A small amount of something bad touches something good, and now the good thing is compromised.
The Three Main Worlds Where "Taint" Lives

1. The Physical World (literal contamination)

In the most concrete sense, you taint a substance — usually food, water, or a material — when you contaminate it with something harmful or impure.

  • The chemical spill tainted the river, making the water unsafe to drink.
  • Leaving the chicken out overnight tainted it with bacteria.
  • One rotten apple can taint the entire barrel.

Notice that in each case, the harmful element doesn't just sit beside the good thing — it gets into it. The river isn't just dirty on the surface; the contamination has entered the water itself.

2. Reputation, Character, and Trust (moral corruption)

This is where "taint" is probably most commonly used in everyday English. When a person's name, image, or character is tainted, it means that something bad — a scandal, an accusation, dishonest behaviour, or a past mistake — has attached itself to that person and damaged how others see them.

  • The fraud charges tainted his reputation permanently.
  • Her involvement in the cover-up tainted her image as an honest politician.
  • The coach's legacy was tainted by the doping scandal.

Here, the person might still be the same person, but a shadow has been cast over them. The way people perceive them has been permanently or seriously changed. People now look at them through a filter of suspicion or doubt.

3. Abstract Things — Judgment, Evidence, Memory, Ideas

Taint also works powerfully on things you cannot touch — things like decisions, reasoning, evidence, or even a memory.

  • His personal hatred for the accused tainted his judgment as a juror.
  • The evidence was tainted because the police had collected it illegally.
  • The trauma she experienced tainted every happy memory she had from that time.

This is perhaps the subtlest use, but also one of the most important. It means that some corrupting influence has entered and distorted something that was supposed to be neutral, reliable, or pure.
A Key Nuance: It Doesn't Mean Total Destruction

One of the most important things to understand about "taint" is that it does not necessarily mean something is completely destroyed or finished. It means it has been compromised — made impure, made untrustworthy, or weakened in its integrity.

For example:

  • Tainted water isn't necessarily black and visibly disgusting. It may look fine but carry harmful bacteria. It has been compromised.
  • A tainted reputation doesn't mean a person has no supporters left. It means there is now doubt, suspicion, or a stain that wasn't there before.
  • Tainted evidence in a courtroom doesn't disappear — but a lawyer can argue it should not be trusted or used.

This makes "taint" a word of quiet but serious damage. It is not explosive; it is corrosive.
Active vs. Passive — Who Does the Tainting?

Active (someone/something taints something else):
Here, there is a clear source doing the corrupting.

  • The company's lies tainted public trust.
  • Greed tainted his otherwise brilliant career.

Passive (something becomes tainted):
Here, the focus is on what has been affected.

  • The food was tainted by poor storage conditions.
  • His whole testimony was tainted by earlier lies he had told.

Both uses are equally common and correct.

There is something slightly invisible and lingering about taint. Unlike words such as "destroy" or "break," which suggest something immediate and obvious, "taint" carries the sense of contamination that seeps in quietly and stays. Once something is tainted, it is very hard — sometimes impossible — to restore its original purity or wholeness in the eyes of others.

This is why "taint" is such a powerful and precise word. It captures that specific, uncomfortable feeling of watching something good become permanently marked by something bad.

To taint = to corrupt, contaminate, or spoil something (a substance, a reputation, a piece of evidence, a memory, a judgment) by introducing something harmful, dishonest, or impure into it — in a way that damages its quality, trustworthiness, or purity, often permanently.
15705: Tainted means something has been contaminated, corrupted, or spoiled in a way that makes it impure, unsafe, untrustworthy, or morally unacceptable. Think of it as a once-clean or once-good thing that has had something bad introduced into it — something that now runs through it like poison through water. The damage is real, serious, and very hard to reverse.
The Key Characteristic: Hidden or Subtle Damage

What makes "tainted" special as a word is that the corruption it describes is often not fully visible on the surface. A tainted piece of meat may look perfectly fine, but it carries harmful bacteria inside. A tainted reputation may belong to someone who appears respectable, but they are associated with wrongdoing underneath. This hidden quality is central to what "tainted" means — it signals that something which may seem okay at first glance is actually compromised in a serious way.
The Different Areas Where "Tainted" is Used

The word "tainted" is flexible. It works in physical, moral, legal, and emotional contexts.

1. Physical / Material Things

When physical substances are tainted, they have been contaminated with something harmful — bacteria, chemicals, toxins, or other pollutants.

  • Tainted food — meat or produce that has been contaminated with dangerous bacteria like E. coli or salmonella. It's unsafe to consume.
  • Tainted water — a water supply that has been polluted with chemicals, industrial waste, or pathogens.
  • Tainted blood supply — blood used for medical transfusions that has been contaminated with a disease.
  • Tainted drugs — medication or street drugs that have been mixed with harmful, foreign substances.

In all these cases, the substance was originally pure but has had something dangerous introduced into it.

2. Reputation and Character

This is one of the most common uses. When a person's reputation is tainted, it means their good name has been damaged or dirtied — usually because of a scandal, wrongdoing, or close association with something shameful.

  • A politician whose reputation is tainted by a corruption scandal.
  • A company whose brand is tainted after it is caught deceiving customers.
  • A celebrity whose image is tainted by allegations of serious misconduct.

Notice that the person doesn't even have to be guilty themselves — sometimes, simply being closely associated with something bad is enough to taint a reputation. This is why people say things like, "His involvement with that fraudulent firm tainted him by association."

3. Evidence and Legal/Official Matters

In law and official proceedings, tainted refers to something that has been compromised, corrupted, or obtained in an improper way — making it unreliable or legally unacceptable.

  • Tainted evidence — evidence gathered by police in an illegal way (e.g., without a proper warrant), which may then be disqualified in court because it cannot be trusted.
  • Tainted jury — a jury that has been improperly influenced, perhaps by media coverage or outside pressure, making a fair trial impossible.
  • Tainted process — an election, vote, or official procedure that has been manipulated or corrupted.

4. Abstract and Emotional Things

"Tainted" is also used to describe feelings, relationships, memories, and other intangible things that have been ruined or permanently darkened by something negative.

  • A tainted memory — a happy memory that is now permanently overshadowed by something painful. For example, a childhood vacation spot might feel tainted after a tragedy happened there.
  • Tainted love — a romantic relationship that has been corrupted by betrayal, obsession, or dishonesty, so that the feeling is no longer clean or healthy.
  • Tainted victory — a win or achievement that feels hollow or wrong because it came through cheating, unfair means, or at someone else's great expense.
  • Tainted joy — happiness that is soured by guilt, regret, or knowledge of something bad.

A critical aspect of the word is that taintedness is very difficult to undo. Unlike something that is merely "dirty" and can be washed clean, something tainted tends to carry its corruption in a lasting way. Once evidence is tainted, it often cannot be used — even if cleaned up. Once a reputation is tainted, the shadow lingers even if the person is later cleared. Once a memory is tainted, it's very hard to remember it the way you used to.

This sense of lasting damage is part of what gives the word its weight and seriousness.
Degree: Slightly Tainted vs. Deeply Tainted

"Tainted" is not an all-or-nothing word. Something can be slightly tainted or deeply tainted. A business deal might be slightly tainted by a small conflict of interest — still largely valid, but not completely clean. A government institution might be deeply tainted by decades of corruption — thoroughly rotten at its core. The word can stretch across a spectrum of severity, and context tells you how severe the taint is.

There are several words close in meaning to "tainted," but each has a slightly different flavour:

  • Contaminated — focuses specifically on physical or chemical pollution. You wouldn't normally say a reputation is "contaminated," but you would say food or water is. "Tainted" works in all these areas.
  • Corrupted — suggests a moral or functional breakdown, often of a system, person, or data. A tainted thing has had something bad introduced from the outside; a corrupted thing has often rotted from within.
  • Spoiled — mostly used for food and relationships; lighter and more everyday than "tainted." Spoiled milk is a minor inconvenience. Tainted meat suggests something more seriously dangerous.
  • Sullied — means dirtied or dishonoured, and is slightly more formal and literary. Tainted is more widely used in everyday language.
  • Compromised — suggests that something has been weakened or made vulnerable, not necessarily made evil. Tainted carries a stronger sense of moral or physical impurity.
  • Poisoned — more extreme and dramatic; implies active harm being caused. Tainted suggests the presence of something harmful, but doesn't always mean harm is being actively inflicted.

It is worth being clear about what the word doesn't mean:

  • It does not mean simply old, worn out, or broken. A tainted thing has had something wrong introduced into it — it isn't just naturally deteriorating.
  • It does not mean merely imperfect. Something can be imperfect without being tainted. Tainted implies a specific kind of corruption or contamination.
  • It does not always mean irreparably destroyed. Something tainted is seriously compromised, but in rare cases — with great effort — the taint can be addressed or reduced (though never fully forgotten).

If you want to carry the essence of this word with you forever, think of it this way:

Tainted = once acceptable or pure, now permanently touched by something harmful, corrupt, or shameful — in a way that is hard to see at first, hard to fix, and impossible to fully forget.

Whether it's tainted food that looks fine but will make you sick, tainted evidence that cannot be trusted in court, or a tainted reputation that follows someone everywhere they go — the word always signals that something has been quietly but seriously compromised.
15706:
To "take a beating" means to suffer serious damage, loss, or defeat. Think of it this way: when someone is beaten up in a fight, they receive many painful blows and come out hurt. The phrase borrows that image and applies it to almost any situation where something or someone suffers badly.

The key word here is seriously. A small scratch is not a beating. A broken arm, a bruised face, a total loss — that is a beating. So whenever you use this phrase, you're saying the damage was significant, not mild.

In its most direct sense, "take a beating" means to be physically hit or punched repeatedly by someone.

Example:
"The fighter took a beating in the third round — he was hit so many times he could barely stand."

Here, the fighter is the one receiving the punches. He is "taking" the beating. The person doing the hitting is giving the beating. These are two sides of the same event.

This literal use still exists, especially in sports like boxing, wrestling, or MMA. But in everyday life, the figurative use is far more common.

This is where the phrase becomes truly powerful. You can apply it to almost anything — money, sports, objects, reputation, your body, your emotions. Whenever something suffers great damage or loss, it has "taken a beating."

Let's look at the most common situations:

1. Financial loss
When money, savings, investments, or a business loses a lot of value or suffers greatly, you say it took a beating.

"My investments took a beating during the economic crisis."
(= My investments lost a lot of money.)

"Small businesses took a beating during the lockdown."
(= Small businesses suffered terribly / many lost money or shut down.)

2. Losing badly in sports or competition
When a team or player is defeated badly — not just by a little, but crushed — they took a beating.

"Our cricket team took a beating yesterday. They lost by 200 runs."
(= They were defeated very badly.)

This is different from just losing. If you lose 51–50, that's a close match. If you lose 100–10, that is taking a beating.

3. Harsh criticism
When a person, book, film, product, or idea is attacked severely by critics or people online, it takes a beating.

"Her debut novel took a beating from reviewers — most called it poorly written."
(= The novel was criticized harshly and repeatedly.)

"The politician's reputation took a beating after the scandal."
(= His reputation was severely damaged.)

4. Physical damage to objects
Objects that are badly damaged by weather, rough use, or accidents can also "take a beating."

"My phone has taken a beating — it's cracked, scratched, and the screen barely works."
(= My phone has been badly damaged over time.)

"Coastal cities take a beating every monsoon season."
(= Coastal cities suffer a lot of damage from rain and floods every year.)

5. Physical exhaustion or strain on the body
When your body goes through something very tough and tiring, you can say your body took a beating.

"After the 10-hour trek, my legs had really taken a beating."
(= My legs were extremely sore and tired.)

"Farmers' bodies take a beating from years of hard physical labour."
(= Their bodies suffer wear and tear from hard work over many years.)

Notice that in all these examples, the "beating" comes from an outside force — a market crash, an opponent, a storm, a critic. The subject is on the receiving end. They didn't choose to be hurt. Something came at them and caused the damage.

This is an important nuance. If a company makes terrible decisions and loses money because of its own mistakes, you can still say it "took a beating," but the phrase fits more naturally when an external force — competition, the economy, nature — is responsible.

Also notice the phrase always implies scale. A beating is not a small inconvenience. It's a serious blow. If your team loses by one goal, you don't say they took a beating. If your stock loses 2%, it didn't take a beating. The word "beating" carries the weight of something significant and painful.

The phrase follows a simple structure:

[Subject] + [took / takes / is taking / has taken / will take] + a beating

Some examples across tenses:

"The economy took a beating last year." (past — it already happened)

"Our local shops are taking a beating because of rising costs." (present continuous — it's happening now)

"If the new policy is implemented, small farmers will take a beating." (future — it might happen)

"Tourism has taken a beating since the floods." (present perfect — it happened and the effect is still felt)

You can also add "from" to show the source of the damage:

"The company took a beating from its competitors."
"My confidence took a beating from all the rejection letters."

"Take a beating" is an informal, everyday expression. You'll hear it in:

  • Sports commentary
  • Financial news reports
  • Casual conversation
  • Newspaper headlines
  • Social media

You would not typically use it in a formal essay, academic paper, or official document. For those settings, you'd say something like "suffered significant losses" or "sustained considerable damage" instead. But in spoken English and most written communication, "take a beating" is perfectly appropriate and widely understood.

These phrases are similar in meaning and you'll often see them used the same way:

"Take a pounding" — Nearly identical to "take a beating." Very common in both physical and financial contexts.
"The currency took a pounding on the foreign exchange market."

"Take a hit" — Similar, but usually suggests a single blow rather than repeated damage. Often implies the situation is still manageable.
"Our profits took a hit, but we recovered quickly." (A hit is less severe than a beating.)

"Take a hammering" — Very common in British English. Means the same thing as take a beating.
"The ruling party took a hammering in the local elections."

"Get thrashed" — Used mostly in sports. Means to be defeated very badly.
"We got thrashed 7–0."

The key difference is that "take a beating" is the most versatile of all these — it works in the widest range of situations (physical, financial, emotional, objects, reputation) and is understood everywhere English is spoken.

The phrase comes directly from boxing and street fighting, where one person receives blow after blow from another. As boxing became popular in the 19th and early 20th centuries, this language naturally spread into everyday speech. People began using "beating" as a metaphor for any kind of painful loss or damage — because defeat in business, sport, or life can feel like being punched repeatedly. The metaphor stuck, and today it is one of the most natural and widely used phrases in the English language.

"Take a beating" = to suffer serious damage, loss, defeat, or harsh criticism.

It works for people, teams, objects, money, reputations, and bodies. It is informal, very common, and always implies the damage is significant — not minor. The subject is always on the receiving end of something painful that came from outside.

Once you know this phrase, you'll start noticing it everywhere — in news headlines, sports commentary, and everyday conversations. It is one of those expressions that, once learned, you will never forget.
15707:
"Take a stab at something" means to try or attempt something, especially when you are not completely sure you will succeed, or when you don't have all the answers.

It is your way of saying: "I'm not certain, but I will give it a try."

Simple definition: To make an attempt at something, even with uncertainty.
The Literal vs. Figurative Meaning

The word "stab" literally means to thrust a sharp object, like a knife, into something — a quick, bold, decisive action.

Now, figuratively, when you "take a stab" at something, you are making a quick, bold attempt at a task, question, or challenge — just like a stabbing motion is fast and direct. You're not hesitating forever. You're just going for it.

So the image is: just as someone thrusts a knife decisively, you thrust yourself decisively into an attempt.
The Most Common Form

The full and most commonly used form of the idiom is:

"Take a stab at (something)"

The word "at" is almost always attached. You take a stab at a problem, at a question, at a task.
Everyday Examples

Here are clear, simple examples showing how it is used in real life:

  1. "I don't know the answer for sure, but let me take a stab at it."

(= I'm not certain, but I'll try to answer.)

  1. "Why don't you take a stab at writing the report first, and I'll review it later?"

(= Just try writing it, even if it's not perfect.)

  1. "She had never cooked Thai food before, but she decided to take a stab at it."

(= She tried it for the first time, without being sure how it would turn out.)

  1. "Nobody wanted to answer the teacher's question, so he took a stab at it."

(= He tried to answer, even though he wasn't fully confident.)

  1. "Let me take a stab at fixing this computer problem."

(= I'll attempt to fix it, though I can't guarantee success.)
The Key Feeling Behind This Idiom

This idiom almost always carries a feeling of uncertainty or humility. When you say "let me take a stab at it," you are quietly signaling:

  • "I might be wrong."
  • "I'm not an expert at this."
  • "But I'll try my best anyway."

It is a very honest and humble expression. It shows confidence in trying without being arrogant about the result.
Origin — Where Did This Come From?

The idiom most likely comes from the physical act of stabbing — a sudden, committed thrust. Historically, a stab was a quick, decisive move. Over time, the language borrowed this image to describe any quick, decisive attempt at something.

There is also a related older expression: "a stab in the dark," which means making a wild guess with almost no information. The two are related in spirit — both involve attempting something with uncertainty — but they are not the same thing (more on this below).
Other Common Variations

The idiom has a few close relatives. All of them mean essentially the same thing:

  • "Have a stab at it" — more common in British English.

"Go on, have a stab at the answer!"

  • "Make a stab at it" — slightly less common, but used in the same way.

"She made a stab at explaining the theory."

  • "Give it a stab" — informal and casual.

"I've never done this before, but I'll give it a stab."

All of these are correct and natural. "Take a stab at it" is the most widely used, especially in American English.
"Take a Stab" vs. "A Stab in the Dark" — Don't Confuse These Two

These two expressions both contain the word "stab," but they are different:

ExpressionMeaning
Take a stab at itTo make an attempt at something (general uncertainty)
A stab in the darkTo make a wild guess with almost no information or clues

Example of the difference:

  • "I'll take a stab at solving this math problem." → You're trying, and you have some idea of how to approach it.
  • "I have no clue what the answer is — that was just a stab in the dark." → You guessed randomly with zero basis.

So "take a stab" is a brave attempt; "a stab in the dark" is a blind guess.
Similar Idioms That Mean the Same Thing

Once you know "take a stab at it," you'll recognize that English has many similar idioms for "trying something":

  • "Give it a shot" — very common and casual. "Give it a shot!"
  • "Give it a go" — more British. "Why not give it a go?"
  • "Take a crack at it" — "Let me take a crack at that puzzle."
  • "Have a go at it" — "Have a go at answering the question."
  • "Take a whack at it" — informal. "Take a whack at solving it."

All of these are interchangeable with "take a stab at it" in most situations.
When Is It Used? (Register & Tone)

"Take a stab at it" is:

  • ✅ Informal and conversational — perfect for everyday speech, casual emails, friendly conversations.
  • ✅ Used in both American and British English, though "have a stab at it" is more British.
  • ✅ Common in workplaces when someone is asked to attempt a draft, a solution, or an answer without pressure.
  • ⚠️ Avoid it in very formal writing — like a legal document or a highly academic paper. In formal contexts, simply say "attempt" or "endeavor."
A Quick Memory Trick

To remember this idiom easily, picture this image:

🎯 A dartboard. You pick up a dart, you're not 100% sure you'll hit the bullseye, but you take a stab — you throw it forward boldly anyway.

That's exactly what the idiom means. A brave, forward attempt, with no guarantee of perfection.
Summary in One Sentence
"Take a stab at something" = to boldly attempt something even when you're not fully confident you'll succeed — and that's perfectly okay.
15708:
When something takes a toll, it means it causes gradual damage, harm, or negative effects — slowly wearing something or someone down over time. It always points to a cost or a loss — not a sudden, one-time hit, but a slow, building burden that leaves something worse than it was before.

Think of it this way: imagine filling a bucket with water, one drop at a time. Each drop seems small, but after a while, the bucket overflows. "Take a toll" describes that kind of slow, accumulating damage.
Where the Word "Toll" Comes From

To truly understand this idiom, you need to understand the word "toll" first.

A toll is a fee or charge you must pay — usually to use a road, a bridge, or a tunnel. When you drive on a toll road, you pay a price for the privilege of using it.

Now, the idiom borrows this idea metaphorically. When hardship, stress, or time "takes a toll" on you, it is as if life is charging you a price — not in money, but in your health, energy, happiness, relationships, or something else valuable. You are being made to pay without choosing to.

There is also a connection to the phrase "death toll," which means the number of deaths caused by a disaster or war. This reinforces the idea that a "toll" is always about loss — something being taken away.
The Full Grammar Structure

The most complete form of the idiom is:

[Something] takes a toll on [someone/something]

  • The subject (the thing doing the harm) comes first.
  • "Takes a toll" is the verb phrase.
  • "On" connects it to the victim or the thing being damaged.

Examples of the full structure:

  • "Stress takes a toll on your heart."
  • "The bad weather took a toll on the harvest."
  • "Years of smoking have taken a toll on his lungs."

You can also drop the "on" part when the context is already clear:

  • "All this travelling is really starting to take a toll." (The listener understands — it's taking a toll on the speaker.)
The Word "Heavy" and Other Intensifiers

You will very often see adjectives placed before "toll" to show how severe the damage is. These are called intensifiers. The most common ones are:

  • a heavy toll — "The war took a heavy toll on the country." (very serious damage)
  • a terrible toll — "The floods took a terrible toll on the village."
  • a serious toll — "Lack of sleep takes a serious toll on concentration."
  • a significant toll — more formal; used in writing and news.

You can also specify what kind of toll it is by adding a descriptive word:

  • a physical toll — damage to the body
  • an emotional toll — damage to your feelings or mental state
  • a mental toll — damage to your thinking or mental health
  • a financial toll — damage to your money or economy

Examples:

  • "Caring for a sick parent takes an enormous emotional toll."
  • "The injury took a physical toll — he never ran as fast again."
What Kinds of Things "Take a Toll"?

The subject — the thing causing the harm — is almost always a force, situation, condition, or ongoing experience, not usually a single person directly harming another. Common subjects include:

  • Stress: "Chronic stress takes a toll on the immune system."
  • Time: "Time takes a toll on all of us."
  • Weather/climate: "Harsh winters take a toll on old buildings."
  • Work/overwork: "Working 80-hour weeks is taking a toll on her marriage."
  • War/conflict: "The civil war took a heavy toll on the economy."
  • Bad habits: "Years of poor diet have taken a toll on his health."
  • Illness: "The long illness took a toll on the whole family."
Key Characteristics — What Makes This Idiom Special

Understanding these three features will help you use it perfectly every time:

1. The damage is almost always gradual.
This idiom rarely describes something that happened in a single moment. It describes wear and tear — like rust slowly eating metal, not a hammer suddenly breaking it.

  • ✅ "Years of arguing took a toll on their friendship." (gradual)
  • ❌ Using it to describe a single sudden accident would feel unnatural.

2. The effect is always negative.
"Take a toll" is never used to describe something good. It always signals harm, loss, decline, or suffering. You will never hear someone say something took a toll and mean it in a positive way.

3. There is an idea of inevitability.
The phrase often carries a feeling that this damage was hard to avoid — it was the natural consequence of circumstances. It doesn't usually imply blame toward a person; it implies that something difficult simply had a cost.
Tense Forms You Will Encounter

Since the damage is often gradual or ongoing, this idiom appears in many tenses. Here are the most common:

  • Present continuous (happening right now, ongoing):

"The long commute is taking a toll on my energy."

  • Simple past (it happened and is done):

"The recession took a toll on small businesses."

  • Present perfect (it happened in the past and the effects are visible now):

"Years of hard work have taken a toll on his body — he looks exhausted."

  • Future (warning that damage will come):

"If you keep skipping sleep, it will take a toll on your health."
Real-Life Contexts Where You'll Hear It

This idiom is extremely common. You'll find it:

  • In news articles: "The economic crisis has taken a heavy toll on the middle class."
  • In everyday conversation: "I haven't been exercising — honestly, it's taking a toll."
  • In health discussions: "Anxiety takes a serious toll on physical health too."
  • In sports: "The injuries have taken a toll on the team this season."
  • In relationship discussions: "The distance took a toll on their relationship."
Similar Expressions (So You Recognise the Idea Elsewhere)

These phrases carry a similar meaning and are often used in the same situations:

  • "Wear someone/something down" — "The stress wore him down over the years."
  • "Leave its mark on" — "The tragedy left its mark on the whole community."
  • "Catch up with someone" — "Years of unhealthy eating finally caught up with him."
  • "Drain" — "The job drains me emotionally."
  • "Exact a price/cost" — more formal; "The campaign exacted a heavy cost on the party."
A Common Mistake to Avoid

Learners sometimes confuse the spelling and write "toll" as "toil" (which means hard work). They are completely different words. Remember:

  • Toll = a fee, a count of losses, or the damage caused (used in this idiom)
  • Toil = to work very hard for a long time

Also, don't say "take a toll to" — it must always be "take a toll on" when followed by a noun.
One-Line Summary to Remember Forever

"Take a toll" means something is slowly causing damage or harm — like a hidden price that life quietly charges you for going through something difficult.

Once you see this idiom in the wild, you'll immediately recognise it: something is happening, and it is costing someone or something dearly — not all at once, but steadily, over time.
15709:
"Take a whack at something" means to try something or to attempt something. That's the heart of it.

If someone says, "Do you want to take a whack at this puzzle?" — they are asking, "Do you want to try solving this puzzle?"
Where Does the Word "Whack" Come From?

To fully understand the phrase, you need to understand the word "whack" first.

"Whack" is an old English word that means a sharp, hard hit or blow. The word itself is onomatopoeic — meaning the word sounds like the action it describes. When you hit something hard and fast — a nail with a hammer, a ball with a bat, a piñata with a stick — the sound it makes is whack!

So in its literal (physical, real-world) sense, "take a whack" means to strike something with force. Imagine a child at a birthday party being told: "Go ahead, take a whack at the piñata!" — that means physically hit the piñata.

Here is where things get interesting.

Over time, people started using "take a whack" in a figurative (non-literal) way. Think about what it looks like when someone takes a hard swing at something: they step up, they put energy into it, they go for it. There's boldness in the action.

That image — of stepping up and going at something energetically — transferred into everyday language. People began saying "take a whack at it" to mean attempt something with energy and willingness, even if no physical hitting is involved.

This kind of shift — from a physical action to a mental or general attempt — is very common in English. Compare:

  • "Take a stab at it" (originally: physically stab) → now: try something
  • "Take a crack at it" (originally: crack/break something) → now: try something
  • "Take a shot at it" (originally: fire a weapon) → now: try something

"Take a whack at it" fits perfectly into this family.
The Full Meaning — What It Really Implies

When someone says "take a whack at something," they don't just mean try. The phrase carries a few extra layers of meaning:

1. It's a willing, active attempt.
You're not being dragged into it. You're stepping up to it, perhaps even with some enthusiasm or confidence.

2. It's usually a first attempt — or one of several.
The phrase suggests you're giving something a go, not that you've already mastered it. It has the spirit of: "I may not succeed, but I'm going to try."

3. It's casual and relaxed.
There's no pressure in this phrase. It doesn't mean "solve this perfectly." It means "have a go at it and see what happens."

4. It suggests the task might have some challenge to it.
You don't usually say "take a whack at drinking this glass of water." You'd say it about something that requires some effort — a problem, a task, a challenge, a creative thing.
Register: When Is This Phrase Used?

This phrase is informal and conversational. You would use it:

  • With friends, family, or colleagues in casual talk
  • In everyday writing like emails or messages
  • In relaxed professional settings

You would not use it in:

  • Formal essays or academic writing
  • Official business documents or reports
  • Highly formal speeches

Think of it as the kind of phrase you'd hear at a dinner table or in an office hallway, not in a courtroom or a university thesis.

The phrase appears in a few forms, and they all mean the same thing:

  • "Take a whack at it" — the most common form in American English
  • "Have a whack at it" — more common in British English
  • "Give it a whack" — also used, same meaning
  • "Take my whack at it" — less common, but heard occasionally

You can also replace "it" with the specific thing you're attempting:

  • "Take a whack at the problem"
  • "Take a whack at the essay"
  • "Take a whack at the recipe"

Here are a wide range of examples to show you how this phrase is used in real life:

At work:

  • "I've been stuck on this report for an hour. Mind if you take a whack at the introduction?"
  • "Nobody's been able to fix this bug. Want to take a whack at it?"

In daily life:

  • "I've never cooked Thai food before, but I'll take a whack at it this weekend."
  • "The drawer is jammed. Here, let me take a whack at opening it."

In learning:

  • "You said the answer is hard to find. Let me take a whack at it anyway."
  • "I don't know the answer, but take a whack at it — there's no harm in guessing."

Encouraging someone:

  • "Don't be nervous. Just take a whack at it and see how it goes."
  • "You'll never know if you don't take a whack at it."

In games or sports:

  • "Everyone gets to take a whack at the piñata."
  • "She took a whack at the ball and sent it flying."

Since English speakers use many phrases to mean "try something," you should know these close relatives of "take a whack at it":

  • "Take a crack at it" — very similar; slightly more common in some regions
  • "Take a shot at it" — implies boldness, also very common
  • "Take a stab at it" — same casual energy
  • "Give it a go" — common in British English, slightly softer
  • "Give it a shot" — very natural and common in American English
  • "Have a go at it" — British-flavored, same meaning
  • "Try your hand at it" — slightly more formal, but same idea

All of these mean make an attempt. "Take a whack at it" sits comfortably in this group — it's one of the livelier, more energetic ways to say it.
What "Take a Whack" Does NOT Mean

A quick note to prevent confusion:

It does not mean you are angry or violent. Even though "whack" literally means to hit, the figurative phrase carries no aggressive meaning at all. It simply means try. The tone is usually warm, encouraging, or casual.

It does not mean you will succeed. It only means you will attempt. Whether you succeed or fail is a separate matter entirely.

It does not mean a half-hearted or lazy try. If anything, it leans slightly toward a confident, energetic attempt — but the emphasis is really just on attempting, not on the quality of that attempt.

"Take a whack at something" means to make an attempt at something, usually in a casual, willing, and somewhat energetic way — it comes from the literal meaning of "whack" (a hard hit) and has evolved into everyday English as a relaxed, informal way of saying "try it."
